summary:
TerraFlame: one consistent fire record for India, 2000 to today

Satellite fire data is hard to compare fairly. MODIS has counted fires since 2000 and VIIRS since 2012, and they see fires differently. When the newer sensor arrives, raw counts jump and year-to-year comparisons break.

TerraFlame, built by team DarkNova, is a fire hotspot calendar for any area in India. Users pick a state, the whole country, a drawn shape or a point and radius. They see detections by year, month or day since November 2000, and whether a period is unusual compared with the same dates in earlier years. A live map shows detections from the last 24 to 72 hours.

We harmonize NASA FIRMS data into one MODIS-equivalent record with an uncertainty band, calibrated by state and month. After conversion, monthly correlation is 0.99 and VIIRS drops from 5.7 times MODIS to 1.03 times. Fresh data arrives every 3 hours, and results can be exported as CSV.
details:
What it does and how it works

TerraFlame is a web app that gives one consistent record of fire hotspot detections for any area of India, from November 2000 to today. A user picks an area: a state, the whole country, a shape drawn on the map, or a point with a radius. They then see detections and fire radiative power (fire intensity) by year, month or day, and whether a chosen period is unusual compared with the same dates in earlier years, shown as a median, percentile and rank. A live map shows individual detections from the last 24, 48 or 72 hours. Results can be downloaded as CSV for an area, a map cell or individual points.

Behind this is a harmonization pipeline. NASA FIRMS has two sensor families that count fires differently: MODIS since 2000 and VIIRS since 2012. When VIIRS arrives, raw counts jump and long-term comparison breaks. We clean the detections, count them per H3 hexagon cell (about 250 km²), per state and per day, and calibrate conversion ratios by state and month using the years both sensors flew. The result is one MODIS-equivalent record with a low-to-high uncertainty band. A scheduled job fetches new detections every 3 hours, harmonizes them the same way, and stores them in PostgreSQL. The website reads only that database, never FIRMS directly.

Benefits

  • History you can compare: old and new satellites sit on one scale, so a jump in the chart is a change in fire activity, not a change of sensor.
  • Answers, not raw data: users get clear readings for their own area and period, like “higher than 96% of earlier years”, instead of files to process.
  • Built-in trust: a Proof page shows how well the converted VIIRS record matches MODIS.
  • Recent and history in one place: the live view and the long-term record sit side by side.

Intended impact

TerraFlame is for emergency managers, forest and agriculture officials, researchers and journalists. They can see quickly whether this season is normal for their area and back decisions with a consistent 25-year record. Open data and an open method mean others can check and reuse the work.

Tools, languages and software

  • Languages: Python and TypeScript.
  • Data and backend: NASA FIRMS API (MODIS and VIIRS), pandas, the H3 hexagon grid, PostgreSQL, FastAPI, and a scheduled ingest job every 3 hours.
  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, ECharts for charts, MapLibre and deck.gl for maps, OpenStreetMap basemap.
  • Design: Figma.

What makes it creative

Most fire tools show either raw recent points or a single sensor’s history. TerraFlame joins the two sensor eras into one record and then shows its own evidence. After conversion, monthly correlation is 0.99 and the typical monthly difference is 8%. VIIRS goes from 5.7 times MODIS to 1.03 times, and 88% of states share the same peak month. A calendar heatmap of years by months makes 25 years of fire seasons readable at a glance. The “is this period unusual” comparison turns statistics into a plain sentence.

Factors our team considered

  • Fairness of comparison: conversion is calibrated per state and per month, not with one national factor.
  • Honesty about uncertainty: every estimate has a low-to-high band. The checks describe the overlap years and are not a forecast.
  • Clear limits: counts are detection events, not unique fires or burned area; clouds, smoke and orbit gaps can hide fires; daily values are noisier than monthly ones.
  • Raw versus converted: map dots are raw FIRMS points, while daily totals are harmonized like the history.
  • Reliability: the app reads only from our own database, so it keeps working if the FIRMS service is slow.
  • Usability and accessibility: plain-language wording, colour-blind-safe chart colours, and light and dark themes.
